speaker: Lisa Blatt
title: Arguing In Front of SCOTUS | Interview: Lisa Blatt
question: In Supreme Court business litigation, why do secondary-liability rulings involving internet platforms matter so much to corporate clients?
guest: Cox is a huge case for two reasons, regardless of how it comes out. It's a case about aiding and abetting, which comes up all the time in various areas of the law, and it's a case about the internet. To me, the outcome in Cox proves and confirms that the internet almost always wins. If it's a case about the internet, the internet just wins, and we'll see how that plays out with AI. But right now, the internet just wins. The aiding and abetting piece, though, is harder, and that is a very important case for businesses more generally, even though the internet is important to a lot of clients. The other thing I watched was the government's position. It is very significant when the government files in these aiding and abetting cases and internet cases because they're not necessarily political, like preemption. It's very important to watch what the government is doing in these types of cases. I don't think the outcome was surprising at all because the minute you start talking about a university and a bunch of kids on the internet, trying to hold someone liable for what a frat house is doing doesn't fly. So it was a great case to watch, and extremely important for aiding and abetting liability.

points.core: The Supreme Court consistently shields internet infrastructure from liability for user misconduct.
points.note: Accept: platforms or ISPs reliably prevailing at SCOTUS because justices resist holding neutral networks responsible for third-party users. Do not credit: generic remarks that tech companies have good lawyers or lobbying power.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Secondary-liability rulings matter because they determine when a company can be held responsible for wrongs committed by its users or customers rather than by the company itself, and that question sets the outer boundary of legal exposure for nearly any business that provides a general-purpose product or service.

For platforms, the scale is enormous: millions of users generate content and conduct that the company cannot individually police, so a loose standard for aiding-and-abetting or contributory liability could mean massive damages, including statutory damages in copyright cases. The Court's recent decisions have generally required culpable, affirmative conduct rather than mere knowledge that some users misuse a service. *Twitter v. Taamneh* (2023) rejected aiding-and-abetting liability for hosting terrorist content through neutral algorithms, and *Cox v. Sony* (2026) limited contributory copyright liability for internet providers.

These rulings reach beyond tech. Their reasoning applies to banks, payment processors, telecoms, manufacturers, and cloud providers, as *Smith & Wesson v. Mexico* (2025) showed. They also shape compliance costs, moderation and account-termination policies, product design, and litigation risk, especially where Section 230 immunity is uncertain.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Supreme Court secondary-liability rulings involving internet platforms matter across corporate America because the Court grounds them in foundational common-law principles that govern virtually every industry, not tech-specific rules. Modern businesses—from banks, manufacturers, and drugmakers to telecom, cloud, and AI providers—supply general-purpose products and infrastructure at massive scale, making some third-party misuse inevitable. If mere knowledge of user misconduct or imperfect policing triggered liability, companies would face existential verdicts, including billion-dollar statutory or treble damages, or have to curtail lawful commerce.

In *Twitter v. Taamneh* (2023) and *Cox Communications v. Sony Music Entertainment* (2026), the Court instead required culpable intent and affirmative participation in wrongdoing rather than passive nonfeasance. Those strict standards cross statutory lines: *Taamneh* directly drove the dismissal of aiding-and-abetting claims against manufacturers in *Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos* (2025). Consequently, platform precedents give corporate defendants powerful leverage to win early dismissals before costly discovery mounts, while compelling corporate rights holders to rethink enforcement against intermediaries.

noweb.answer: Supreme Court rulings on internet-platform secondary liability matter deeply to corporate clients because the doctrines they establish reach far beyond technology companies. Primary wrongdoers—such as terrorists, counterfeiters, or infringers—are often overseas or judgment-proof, giving plaintiffs strong incentives to target solvent intermediaries for massive statutory or treble damages. When the Court defines aiding-and-abetting or contributory liability in platform disputes like *Twitter v. Taamneh*, it typically construes general statutes and traditional common-law tort principles rather than internet-specific rules, meaning those precedents equally govern banks, payment processors, shippers, telecoms, and manufacturers. For any business providing routine, arms-length goods or services at scale, the crucial question is whether general awareness that bad actors might misuse its infrastructure triggers liability, or whether plaintiffs must plead conscious, culpable participation in specific wrongdoing. Loose standards turn ordinary commerce into de facto insurance for third-party misconduct—letting expansive claims survive motions to dismiss and forcing costly discovery and coercive settlements—whereas strict thresholds keep compliance duties and litigation exposure predictable.

Corporate clients care about these rulings because the decisions set how much legal risk a company carries for what millions of strangers do with its products. Platforms, internet providers, payment processors and software vendors can't screen every user. So whether "aiding," "contributory" or "inducement" liability needs real intent and active participation, or just general knowledge that some users misbehave, decides whether their basic business model is legally safe.

The recent cases show how much is at stake. In Twitter v. Taamneh (2023), the Court said hosting ISIS content and running recommendation algorithms didn't amount to "knowingly providing substantial assistance" under the Anti-Terrorism Act. On March 25, 2026, in Cox v. Sony, it ruled unanimously that an internet provider isn't contributorily liable for its subscribers' piracy unless it induced the infringement or offered a service built for it. That wiped out a $1 billion verdict.

These standards spread to other areas of law, and the damages that could come from vast numbers of users are enormous. The rulings shape how companies design products and run compliance and moderation programs. They also affect insurance, settlement leverage and whether a company can get a case dismissed early instead of facing a jury.

Secondary-liability rulings decide when a company can be held responsible for wrongs committed by *other people* who use its products or services. Internet platforms are the test cases because they serve billions of users, so the exposure is enormous. A rule that a platform "aids and abets" terrorism or contributes to infringement merely by providing generic services to the public would mean potentially unlimited liability for conduct the company never directed.

The principles also reach well beyond tech. In *Twitter v. Taamneh* (2023), the Court held that aiding-and-abetting liability requires conscious, culpable participation in a specific wrong, not just arm's-length provision of widely available services with general awareness of misuse. That standard applies to banks, payment processors, telecom carriers, shipping firms, and suppliers. Copyright disputes such as *Cox v. Sony* raise the parallel question of contributory infringement for internet service providers.

For corporate clients, these rulings shape litigation risk, compliance and monitoring obligations, insurance costs, and the viability of business models. They also influence how lower courts read common-law tort principles that run across many federal statutes.
